titulo.texto: Peoples of Maize and Stone, and the Olmec Phenomenon

frase_gancho.texto: Figurines, vessels and an incense burner shaped like a catfish: this is how life begins in the villages of Morelos more than three thousand years ago.

puente_narrativo.texto: Continue through the palace: go up to the terrace where the cuexcomate stands.

guion_corto.texto: About three thousand five hundred years ago, the communities of Morelos already lived by growing maize. The Peoples of Maize and Stone hall displays female figurines, bottles and cooking pots dated between fifteen hundred and twelve hundred BC. These are everyday objects, not luxury goods. In the next hall, The Olmec Phenomenon, something else appears: the influence of a Gulf Coast culture on the pottery and sculpture of Morelos. Among the pieces are the Oaxtepec vessel and an incense burner shaped like a catfish. There is also a replica of Monument thirty-six from Chalcatzingo, a site in Morelos with stone reliefs. Here the museum speaks of villages, not kings.

guion_largo.texto:
These two halls tell the same story in two tones. The first is about daily life; the second, about ideas that traveled.

In Peoples of Maize and Stone, the museum brings together objects from communities that lived in Morelos between fifteen hundred and twelve hundred BC. There are female clay figurines, bottles and cooking pots. The figurines are among the most common objects of that era in Mesoamerica. What they were for is still debated. Some specialists link them to fertility or to household rituals. The pots and bottles are easier to read. They were for cooking, storing and serving.

The title of the hall speaks of maize and stone for a reason. Maize was the basis of food and of life for Mesoamerican peoples. Stone was the material of tools and, later, of sculptures and temples. Between the two, a stable way of life takes shape.

The second hall is called The Olmec Phenomenon. The Olmec were a culture of the Gulf Coast of the Gulf of Mexico, famous for their colossal heads. Their influence reached many regions, including Morelos. In the hall there is pottery and sculpture from Morelos that show traits of that style.

Among the most important pieces is the Oaxtepec vessel. Another is an incense burner shaped like a catfish, that is, a river fish with whiskers. And there is a replica of Monument thirty-six from Chalcatzingo. Chalcatzingo is an archaeological site in Morelos with reliefs carved into the rocks of a hill. When the museum shows a replica, it is because the original stayed in its place.

The word influence is important. Specialists debate how the Olmec style reached Morelos: whether through trade, through the travels of people, or through an exchange of ideas. What can be seen in the display cases is that local communities made their own version.

The museum points to Xochicalco as the most important archaeological site among those it presents. Xochicalco is an ancient city of Morelos, built on a hill and much later than the villages of this hall. The two eras live side by side in the museum and show how long the thread of the state’s history is.

One way to look at the two halls together is to ask what changes and what stays. The objects and the styles change. Clay, maize and the need to store, cook and share stay.

The tour through these halls leaves a question worth taking with you to the rest of the museum. In the year fifteen hundred BC there were already villages with pots, figurines and shared styles. So, what was there before the tecpan, the Tlahuica plaza and the Palace of Cortés? Much more history than is usually told. If you have time, look again at a vessel or a figurine and think of the hands that made it. Each piece was made by a person, for a specific use.

texto: Find the Oaxtepec vessel and the incense burner shaped like a catfish and compare them: which looks like it was for daily use and which for ceremony?
Find the female figurines and notice how the artist handled the face and the body
Look at the replica of Monument thirty-six from Chalcatzingo and think about why a copy is displayed

texto.pregunta: Myth: The Olmec were the founders of all the cultures of Mesoamerica.
texto.respuesta: Reality: Specialists debate how much they influenced others. In Morelos their influence can be seen, but the local communities made their own style.
